summary: Defines a YANG data model for configuring and managing the Network Time Protocol, version 4, and it can also manage version 3. The model covers both configuration data and operational state data, so management tools can set up and monitor time synchronization consistently. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Computers need to agree on what time it is. This is a standard settings form that lets one control program set up and check the clocks on many machines.

subtitle: A standard YANG schema for configuring NTP on a device and reading back its time-sync state.

tldr.problem: Every NTP implementation has its own way to be configured and monitored, which makes managing time synchronization across devices from different vendors awkward.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9249 defines the YANG module ietf-ntp. It has one top-level container that holds NTP configuration (access rules, authentication keys, unicast and per-interface settings) and read-only state (clock status, associations, statistics).
tldr.outcome: Management tools using NETCONF or RESTCONF can configure and monitor NTP version 4, and version 3, through one common data model.

today: RFC 9249 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2022. It does not obsolete or update any other RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What the Module Covers
sections.content:
RFC 9249 defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage Network Time Protocol version 4 (RFC 5905). The model can also be used for NTPv3 (RFC 1305). YANG is the data modeling language of RFC 7950.

The configuration side covers system parameters of NTP such as access rules, authentication and VPN Routing and Forwarding (VRF) binding, the various NTP modes, and per-interface parameters. It also gives access to the running state of an NTP implementation.

Operational state lives in the same tree as configuration, consistent with the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342). Current state, statistics and the state of each NTP association are all included. The terminology follows RFC 5905 and RFC 1305, and the tree diagrams use the notation of RFC 8340.
sections.eli5: NTP is how computers learn the right time. This document is a standard form for filling in NTP's settings and for asking a computer how its clock is doing.

sections.title: The ietf-ntp Data Model
sections.content:
The module is called ietf-ntp and has one top-level container, ntp, which holds both configuration and running state. Its main parts are:

  • port: the port used to send NTP packets (an optional feature).
  • refclock-master: configures the device as a reference clock with a given stratum.
  • authentication: whether authentication is enabled, and the list of authentication keys.
  • access-rules: on-the-wire access control.
  • clock-state: read-only system status such as clock state, stratum and reference ID.
  • unicast-configuration: configured unicast servers and peers.
  • associations: read-only list of current associations, each with its own ntp-statistics.
  • interfaces: per-interface broadcast, multicast and manycast server and client settings.
  • ntp-statistics: global statistics.

There is also one RPC, statistics-reset, that resets the statistics either for one association or for all of them.

Many parts are optional YANG features, so a device can implement only some of them: for example ntp-port, authentication, access-rules, unicast-configuration, and separate features for broadcast, multicast and manycast servers and clients. The full tree is in Appendix A of the RFC.
sections.eli5: All the settings live in one big folder called ntp. Inside are drawers for clock settings, passwords, who may ask for the time, and a read-only page showing how the clock is doing.

sections.title: Relationship to the NTPv4 MIB and RFC 7317
sections.content:
If a device implements the NTPv4-MIB (RFC 5907), the YANG data nodes can be mapped to its table entries. The RFC gives two tables. For example, clock-stratum corresponds to ntpEntStatusStratum, and the per-association offset corresponds to ntpAssocOffset. Packet counters under ntp-statistics map to ntpAssocStatOutPkts, ntpAssocStatInPkts and ntpAssocStatProtocolError.

RFC 7317 already has a small NTP section under /system/ntp. The new model supports per-interface configuration, which that one does not. If the model of RFC 9249 is implemented, /system/ntp SHOULD NOT be used and MUST be ignored. A third table maps the old nodes to the new: unicast-configuration replaces server, and its address, port, type, iburst and prefer nodes line up with the matching nodes in /system/ntp.
sections.eli5: There was an older settings form and an older monitoring format. This document says which new box matches which old one, and says to stop using the old settings form once you use the new one.

sections.title: Access Rules, Keys and NTP Version
sections.content:
Access rules control who may reach the NTP service on the wire. They are independent of management access control such as NACM. Each rule uses one of four access modes, and each mode can have its own access control list from RFC 8519:

  • Peer: others may synchronize with this entity and vice versa; control queries are accepted. This is the full access authority.
  • Server: others may synchronize with this entity, but not vice versa; control queries are accepted.
  • Server-only: like server, but control queries are not accepted.
  • Query-only: only control queries are accepted. This is the most restricted mode.

Key management follows the NTP specifications. When authentication is enabled, NTP uses a crypto-checksum together with predistributed keys indexed by a 32-bit unsigned key identifier (keyid). The keyid MUST be configured on the NTP peers before authentication can be used, and it is named when an association is configured. The module marks key data with nacm:default-deny-all to prevent retrieving the actual key once it is set. A deprecated feature covers MD5, SHA-1 and other deprecated mechanisms for legacy compatibility.

The module also lets the operator choose NTPv3 or NTPv4 for each association, for backward compatibility with legacy systems. The RFC notes that NTPv3 is obsoleted by NTPv4.
sections.eli5: You can decide who is allowed to ask your computer for the time, from just asking questions, all the way to trading time both ways. Secret keys with numbers prove the messages are real, and the keys cannot be read back after you set them.

sections.title: Usage Examples
sections.content:
Section 9 shows NETCONF edit-config and get requests for common jobs. They are for illustration.

  • A preferred unicast server at 192.0.2.1 on port 1025, using authentication key 10 and the default NTP version 4, and the same with an IPv6 address.
  • A reference clock with stratum 8.
  • Turning on authentication with trusted key 10 using AES-CMAC and a hexadecimal key string.
  • Access configuration for a peer access mode.
  • A multicast server with address 224.0.1.1, port 1025, version 3 and keyid 10, plus multicast client, manycast client and manycast server setups.
  • Reading back the clock state, all associations, and global statistics.
sections.eli5: The document shows sample messages, like a recipe: how to tell a computer which time server to trust, and how to ask it how well its clock is doing.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed with NETCONF or RESTCONF. NETCONF's mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH, and RESTCONF's is TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) can restrict which users may do what, and key information is protected with nacm:default-deny-all.

Writable nodes can hurt if changed without protection. Changing /ntp/port, /ntp/unicast-configuration or /ntp/interfaces/interface could disrupt the network, and the interface settings could even lead to synchronizing to an untrusted source instead of trusted ones. Readable nodes are sensitive too. Unauthorized access to the authentication keys could be exploited to gain access to the NTP service, and the association list could reveal network topology or trust relationships. The statistics-reset RPC could be abused to disturb monitoring.

The key algorithm leaf can be set to algorithms that are no longer secure. According to RFC 8573, AES-CMAC is the recommended algorithm.

IANA registered the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ntp in the IETF XML Registry and the module name ietf-ntp with prefix ntp in the YANG Module Names registry.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change these settings could mess up your clocks, and anyone who can read the secret keys could pretend to be a trusted time source, so only the right people should be allowed in.
